questions.question: Why is Naive Bayes called 'naive'?
options: Because it assumes all features are independent given the class label.
Because it can only handle binary classification.
Because it doesn't require any training data.
Because it is the simplest possible algorithm in existence.
questions.explanation: The 'naive' part refers to the strong (and usually false) assumption that the presence of one word is completely independent of the presence of another, given the class.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'negation scoping' in sentiment analysis?
options: To distinguish between words like 'good' and 'NOT_good' so the classifier can weight them differently.
To remove all negative words from the text.
To find the scope of a mathematical equation in the text.
To count how many 'not' words appear in a sentence.
questions.explanation: Negation scoping helps simple classifiers handle phrases like 'not good' by treating words following a negation as distinct features (e.g., 'NOT_good'), preventing them from being confused with their positive counterparts.

questions.question: Why is Macro-F1 often preferred over Accuracy for evaluating sentiment models?
options: It respects class imbalance by giving equal weight to minority and majority classes.
It is always a higher number than accuracy.
It only measures the performance of the positive class.
It doesn't require a ground truth label.
questions.explanation: Accuracy can be misleading if one class (e.g., positive reviews) is much larger than another. Macro-F1 averages the F1 scores of each class equally, highlighting poor performance on minority classes.

questions.question: In which case would you likely need to switch from a classical linear model to a transformer?
options: Detecting sarcasm or subtle shifts in sentiment mid-document.
Classifying 10,000 movie reviews with clear 'loved it' or 'hated it' language.
When memory and latency are extremely constrained.
When you only have 100 labeled examples.
questions.explanation: Transformers are better at capturing long-range dependencies, sarcasm, and complex linguistic nuances that bag-of-words or linear models typically miss.
